newsitem.title: UK: EMU stability pact offers no bail-out - EC adviser.
newsitem.headline: EMU stability pact offers no bail-out - EC adviser.

text.p: Budgetary plans of EMU members will be monitored by the European central bank, but there will be no bail-out if that early warning system fails, a European Commission adviser said on Thursday.

"The community budget is barely 1.3 percent of the GDP of its union," said Andre Louw, economic adviser at the European Commission (EC), speaking at a conference in London. "That is insufficient to alleviate financial difficulties which result from divergent fiscal policies."
The Commission said earlier it had adopted proposals for a stability pact designed to ensure lasting budget discipline.
Members of European Economic and Monetary Union will have to submit medium-term policy plans to the central bank in order to allow any potential problems to be spotted.

Louw said member states were not allowed under the terms of EMU to go to the aid of any country which had allowed itself to fall out of line, although there would clearly be pressure for them to do so.
"It is essential that those countries which join are not likely to present that kind of risk," he said. "The stability pact must be respected."

In accepting EMU, a member state was losing the right to devalue its currency in the light of wage and price developments, he said. They must therefore be able to remain competitive in relation to other members.
"If they are uncompetitive, the only thing they can do is push nominal wages and prices down," said Louw. "Premature entry into EMU carries an important risk."
According to the stability pact, an overshoot of the budget deficit requirement -- which must not exceed 3.0 percent of GDP -- will only be accepted if it is "temporary and exceptional".
However, Louw said the meaning of those terms was still subject to debate and was likely to be settled later this year.
Member countries would have to pay a non-remunerative deposit, which would become a fine if they exceeded the target.
The fine would be 0.2 percent of GDP plus 0.1 percent of the amount in excess of 3.0 percent deficit to GDP target ratio, up to a cap of 0.5 percent of GDP, the European Commission said.
